column2: the writer's notes (doubts; where the article disagrees with the entry): for the data check

The article does not say when or how the shared lordship with his brothers and cousin ended; the text says only that he ended up as sole ruler. Parma's later sale to Luchino Visconti (in the entry) is not in the article and is not repeated.

The article says the siege of Greifensee was laid in May 1444 and the town taken after four weeks on 27 May, which is inconsistent; the text gives only the year and the four weeks. The entry dates the war 1440-1446; the definitive peace of 1450 is told as its aftermath.

The entry says Agathocles had him killed; the article says Agathocles attacked his camp and he died fighting. Both are compatible and the text follows the article. Athens is given as the homeland of his wife Eurydice, from where he gathered his army.

The entry says the debate was planned for Rome; the article does not name the place, so the text does not either. The article's claim that the 900 theses were the first printed book universally banned by the Church was left out.

The entry's Southern Xiongnu and Tangut settlement are not in the article and are not repeated. The article mixes the names Ordosian culture (Palaeolithic) and Ordos culture (bronze-age nomads); the text keeps them apart as the article's later sections do.

The entry calls the deposits one of the largest in the world; the article calls them the world's largest. The text gives the estimates with whose they are and makes no ranking of its own. The 2007 nationalisation in the entry is not in the article; the 60% PDVSA share agrees with it. Projected outputs and commissioning dates of the blocks were left out as forecasts.

The article gives c. 1677 for his return to Kwaaman but says he ruled Kwaman from c. 1680; the text gives no year for his accession. Versions differ on whether the affair was with the Denkyirahene's sister or niece Akobena Abensua or with the queen of Nkawie; the text names neither. The article calls the stool a wooden stool partly covered with gold; the entry's name, the Golden Stool, is not repeated.
The article gives his death as between 3 May 1289 and 19 March 1290, which agrees with the entry's d. c. 1290.
The article gives his birth as likely around 1585; the entry's dates say c. 1590. The text gives no birth year.

The entry dates the founding of Demetrias to 294 BCE; the article gives 290 or 293 BCE. The text gives no year. The article gives no year for Philip II's conquest; the entry's 352 BCE is not repeated.

The article gives two different urban populations (1,435,210 or 48%, and 1,561,438 or 52.22%); the text gives neither. The article's date of 1564 for about nine large churches in Vasai taluka reads oddly ('built during 1564') and was left out. Political office holders were left out.
The entry's mention of the Ionian Revolt councils is not in the article and is not repeated.
The entry dates the post's creation to no later than Leo IV, as the article does.

The article gives the oldest colophon's date as 1522 Saka (1600 CE) and calls the work a 16th-century chronicle; the entry says the oldest manuscripts date from the early seventeenth century. The text gives only the span 1481-1600 for the writing of its final part and no manuscript date.

The entry says the party ruled as a one-party state from 1962; the article says it was the only legal party by 1965. The text gives neither date for the one-party state. The entry says the party was founded in 1959 from Kayibanda's earlier movement; the article says the movement was founded in June 1957 and renamed in 1959. The text gives both steps, which agree with the entry.

The article says he served five of his twelve years, but also that he was jailed in February 1986 and released on 29 May 1990; the text gives only the sentence and the release date. His term in the House of Assembly for St. Joseph in 1985-86 and the unclear account of the Labour deputy leadership were left out.
The entry names the Serbian ruler Đurađ Branković; the article calls him George Branković, and the text follows the article.
The article gives his birth as June 1485; the entry's dates say 1493. The text gives no birth year.
The article is short; the text uses nearly all of it. The Cessetani in the entry are not in the article.

Village spelled Mala Pereshchepyna in the article, Malaya Pereshchepina in the entry; used the article's spelling in the text, the entry's name stands as aka. The 2019 display: article says the sword was presented in Sofia by Boyko Borisov to Audrey Azoulay; kept only the date and Sofia.

The article says the consortium collapsed in 1343 and was bankrupt in 1345; the entry gives bankruptcy in 1343, so I give only the collapse of 1343 and leave 1345 out. The article's lead puts a restructuring with outside capital in the 1340s as the start of a quarter-century of prosperity, which contradicts the 1343 collapse (probably the 1300s); left out. Article: the war with France and England 'over Aquitaine' is its wording; the Planters company and American dealerships left out as off-topic.

Article dates the Haudenosaunee raids on the Wendat to 1648-1649 and the turn on the Petun to the end of 1649; the entry has 1649-1650 for the Petun dispersal, so I give only 'by the end of 1649' and no end year.

The entry says Phetracha executed Phaulkon; the article says Phaulkon was executed by Phetracha's son Luang Sorasak on 5 June. I wrote 'Phaulkon on 5 June' without naming the executioner. The article says Ayutthaya received white elephants from Cambodia and mediated between Vientiane and Luang Prabang; left out for length.

SKIPPED: the article is about the modern regional unit of Phocis (geography, prefecture, municipalities, population, football clubs); its sections on the ancient, Byzantine and Frankish history are empty, so it has nothing on the ancient region the entry describes

The article says 'later in 1739' a son of his was killed in battle with the Ojibwe and Dakota and quotes his outburst; this seems to confuse the death of Jean-Baptiste in 1736 (killed by the Sioux on Massacre Island, given earlier in the article). Left the 1739 passage and the quotation out. Article says he 'received a cadet's commission at twelve' and took part in raids of 1704-1705; I avoided ages and gave the raids without years.

The article's lead says the Hohenzollerns governed their Franconian lands from the castle from 1340 'till 1604', while its history section says the residence moved to Bayreuth in 1542 and the castle remained the administrative centre until after the middle of the 16th century; I gave 1340 and 1542 only and left 1604 out. Article calls Albert II 'Albert II of Brandenburg-Kulmbach'; Albert Alcibiades is the same person but the article does not say so, so I did not equate them.
The entry mentions a Polish naval victory at Oliwa in 1627; the article mentions only that the Poles recaptured Oliwa in late November 1627, with no naval battle. I did not mention Oliwa.
The article says Díaz was 'forced to resign and go into exile' without giving the year in the given text; the entry's 1911 end stands.

The entry says Britain obtained the area from the Mpondo in 1878; the article says Nqwiliso ceded the western bank to the Cape Colony on 17 July 1878. I followed the article's wording (the Cape Colony was British) and did not mention 1894.

The article gives contradictory dates: the dynasty founded in 546 BCE and ruling 546-408 BCE, Pālaka ruling c. 659-635 BCE (Merutunga), and Pradyota campaigning against Vatsa around 495 BCE despite a 23-year reign from 546. I left all precise years out; the entry gives only 6th-5th century BCE. The article's list of five kings ruling 138 years and the Aryaka overthrow come from different traditions; I kept both without reconciling.
Two sections only; the article has nothing on its history beyond the origin as a way of preserving fish, which the entry already gives.

The article gives his birth as c. 1599 and his death as 1655 in the lead, then 1656 (some sources 1655) later; the entry has c. 1600-1656 and a reign to 1656. I gave neither birth nor death year. The entry says the Japanese soldiers had supported his rivals; the article says Yamada first allied with him, then objected to his taking the throne and rebelled. I told the events without that characterisation.

The entry says only a fragment of one of his choral songs survives; the article speaks both of 'a considerable fragment' of a hyporcheme in Athenaeus and of 'some interesting fragments of his hyporchemes'. I mention only the one passage in Athenaeus and do not say how many fragments survive. Article: monument erected 'in honor of him' - ambiguous whether Aristias or Pratinas; I wrote 'in his honour' after Aristias, following the article's sentence order.

The article cites 'the writing of Pope Pius II in 1509', impossible as Pius II died in 1464; left out. The article says the stone went to the Landhaus in 1862 and was displayed at the State Museum from 1905; kept both as given. Removed in the article's present-day line: Jörg Haider's name as governor; kept only the 2006 move.

The article says construction began in the 6th century and continued over the next 400 years, but elsewhere that the phases ran 'over three centuries during the Terminal Classic Period'; the entry gives 6th to 10th century. I gave only the dates of individual temples. Left out the article's speculative numerology about the base ratio and the golden ratio.
The entry calls him the elder brother of Alp Arslan; the article does not say which was older, so I did not repeat it.

The entry says he helped Song conquer Southern Tang; the article says only that he took part in the annexation of the other small southern kingdoms, which I followed. The article reports his death after drinking the emperor's wine without calling it poisoning; I did the same.

The entry says the Later Liang made him king of Wuyue in 907; the article says Emperor Taizu created him Prince of Wuyue. I wrote 'the title of Wuyue' without prince or king. The article says 'after Qian Liu killed Dong Chang' but the given excerpt does not tell how; I wrote only that he destroyed him and gave no date for it.

The article places the find at the Rabatak pass on the border of Baghlan and Samangan provinces; the entry says Baghlan Province. Province not repeated. Mukherjee reads a Saddashkana where Sims-Williams reads Vima Taktu; the relationships of the kings left as in the entry.

The article dates his refusal of Clovis and his death to 509; the entry says 'around 509' and 'd. c. 509'. Year left out of the text. The article spells the brother Ricchar (Riccar), the entry Richar: brother left unnamed in the text.

The article dates Sánchez's execution both 4 July 1861 and July 1863; left out. Article gives his name as Matías Ramón Mella and says the evidence for that form is thin; the entry's name kept, the documents' form reported as such.
The article names his killer as his son Udaysimha (Udai Singh I); the entry says Udai Karan. Son left unnamed. Article: Vijay Stambha completed probably 1458-1468, some sources 1448.
The article dates his accession to 20 February 1856 (Gulab Singh's abdication) and his reign from 1856; the entry says he succeeded his father in 1857. Accession year left out of the text.
The article gives her regency both as 1527-1533 and as beginning when Vikramaditya succeeded after 1531; regency dates left out. Jauhar on 8 March 1535 agrees with the entry but is already in it.

The article says the river opens into the head of the Adriatic; the entry says the Bay of Raša on the Kvarner Gulf. Not contradictory, but Kvarner not repeated. The article gives 129 without era; taken as BCE from context (a generation after 177 BC).

The article's lead says the voivodeship lasted until the partitions of 1795, its body that Prussia annexed it in the second partition of 1793; the entry's 1793 kept. The entry lists Sochaczew among the lands from 1462; the article says Sochaczew returned in 1476 - not contradictory with the entry's wording, so kept.
The article also mentions the Wagon Box Fight but its excerpt gives no detail; left out.
The article gives no single birthplace; several claims summarised without choosing.
The article dates the Canadian purchase both 1869 generally and 1 December 1869 as the planned transfer date; text says Canada agreed to buy without a date.
The article quotes the motto as 'Labour, Family, Fatherland'; the entry has 'Work, Family, Fatherland'. Motto not repeated.
The article gives his birth as the 1130s; the entry c. 1130. No birth year in the text.
The entry places the movement's origin in Kham; the article says it became established in the Kingdom of Derge. Not contradictory.
The article dates the Itamaraty Peace Declaration to 1995 as the final resolution; the entry gives a final settlement of 1998. No year given for the final settlement in the text.

The entry says the 1102 rebellion failed when his Welsh allies under Iorwerth ap Bleddyn changed sides; the article says only that Henry besieged and captured his English castles. Welsh allies not mentioned.

The article dates the Bayonet Constitution's coming both to 1887 (the '1887 Document', his recall in August 1887) and to the Reform Party taking power in 1888; no year given for it in the text. He was called home on 29 August 1887 per the article.
The article dates Tupac Amaru II's uprising to 1758 (a slip, it says 'more than 150 years later' after 1609); year left out.

The entry says the caliph gave the honorific in 946; the article says al-Mustakfi gave the three brothers their titles after Ahmad took Baghdad in 945. The year of the title is left out. The article dates his death to September 976; the entry gives d. 976. Only the year and 'a few months later' are used.

The entry dates his death to 1257; the article gives his life as 1230-1256 and says he was killed in 1256. The year of his death is left out of the text. The Persian historian Juvayni, hostile to the Nizaris, is the article's main contemporary source; not stressed in the text.

The Pechenga raid is dated 25 December 1589 in the article, before the war's start in 1590; kept with its date as the article gives it. The entry names Korela among the towns returned; the article says Teusina restored everything ceded at Plussa except Narva, without naming the towns. The list of towns returned is not repeated.

The article dates his marriage to 1788 and says the society he founded with his wife's connections was disbanded in 1787; the year of the marriage is left out because of this inconsistency. The entry says he served as ambassador to France and Britain; the article confirms both.

The article's lead dates his rule as Nawab from 26 January 1722 but its body dates his appointment to Awadh 9 September 1722; the body's date is used, matching the entry's 1722. The article names him Saadat Khan; the entry's name Saadat Ali Khan I and title Burhan-ul-Mulk refer to the same man.
The Ghaznavid celebrations in the entry are not in the article; not used. The article states the Achaemenid origin flatly, without a source named.

The article dates the stupa near the museum to the second century BC and also says it was possibly built by Ashoka; the date is left out, as the two may not agree. The article does not say that the Walis made the town their capital or built its schools and hospitals (the entry does); not repeated or contradicted. The college ranking in the article is left out under the guide's rules.

The article gives his death as 460 and his birth in the 4th century; the entry says he lived probably in the 5th or 6th century. No year of life or death is given in the text. The article says the Vita was 'written by Dom Plaine around 1220-1235'; Dom Plaine's name is left out as doubtful in that pairing, the date kept. The article's paragraph on Celtic aquaculture and the meaning of the legend is interpretive and unsourced; left out.

The entry says the town of Mons grew around the community she founded; the article's wording ('The city of Mons grew around it', after Ghislain's oratory at Ursidongus) is ambiguous, so the text does not say what Mons grew around.

The article gives his birth as 17 June 1934; the entry's dates are 1935–1978. The birth date is left out. The article places the prime ministers' terms (to August 1971) after the 1975 merger, out of order; told in date order here.

The article gives the area of the Zenú works as both about 50,000 and 20,000 square kilometres, and a drainage basin of 96,500 square kilometres in south-eastern Córdoba, which seems far too large; all these figures are left out. The article flows the river into the Cauca in Sucre; the entry says it joins the Magdalena river system in La Mojana. The Cauca is not contradicted, but La Mojana is not named in the article. The tributary given in the article as 'Dirty' (presumably a mistranslation) is left out.

The article's account of the icon of the Virgin of the Staircase and its replica in the Philippines is long and loosely sourced; left out. The article says the fort saw no action after the 1560s under Spanish control, which sits oddly with the Spanish holding it until 1825; not repeated.

The entry dates the founding to around 1299; the article says the 1299 date was William Linehan's 1947 reckoning, since discredited, that the Annals give no dates, and that Valentijn and van der Vorm reckoned 1160 and 1177. The article also gives his death in 1347 after 48 years, which implies 1299. All founding and death dates are left out. The entry says the dynasty's last king founded Malacca; the article discusses whether Parameswara and Iskandar Shah were one person or father and son. Not repeated. The article spells the minister both Demang Lebar Daun and Demang Lebar Dawn; the first is used.
The article's lead says 'founded in the late-8th century' while its history section says around 760, the entry's date; the text uses around 760.

The article gives his birth as c. 1918-1920; the entry's c. 1918 is not repeated in the text. The article dates the Iranian landing on the islands to 30 November 1970, which sits oddly with its own 'following the evacuation of the British'; the date is left out. Rankings (oldest reigning monarch, largest bulk port) left out under the guide's rules.
The article calls him Adi Kabi, the First Poet; the entry's 'father of Odia literature' is consistent and not repeated.
The article dates the public recital to 'the following year' (1905) after publication on 16 August 1904; the publication date is the entry's and is not repeated.

The entry says it had hundreds of thousands of members by 1919; the article gives 350,000 in 1916 (other estimates 800,000, or a claimed million) and an SI claim of 2 million in 1919. Membership figures are left out.

The entry says Ieyasu moved him to Akita in 1602; the article says the clan arrived in its new domain in 1603. Neither year is given in the text. Kubota Castle (entry) is not in the article; not mentioned. The article's claim that he was counted among the six greatest Toyotomi generals is left out as a ranking.
The article dates the start of his reign to 432 BC; the entry gives 433. The year is left out. The Sindian king's name is kept as the article spells it, Hecactaeus.
The trial and the March regulation fall in 1914, but the article gives no year for them, so none is printed.
The article names the historian only as Mahon.
SKIPPED: article under 300 words, mostly an empty family tree; it adds little beyond the description
The article dates the Battle of Sekigahara to 1601; no year printed for it. The entry's 'until 1871' is not in the article (it says partly dismantled in the 1870s).
Kept the article's '3rd century BC and the 16th century AD' as BCE/CE.
The entry calls Mehmed Sokolović grand vizier at the restoration of 1557; the article says he was a vizier from 1555 and became Grand Vizier in 1565. His title is left out.
The entry dates the hiring of the Ten Thousand to 400–399 BCE; the article says the winter of 401/400 BC. No date is printed for it.
The article gives Herzfeld's surname only.
The entry's oil exports of 1962 are not in the article. Thin article; text kept to what it gives.
The article gives several datings (c. 360–285, c. 395–315 BCE in Chinese sources, c. 350–275 in the West); none is printed, as the entry gives c. 350–275 BCE.
The article gives his accession both as 18 January and 27 January 1841; only January 1841 is printed. Its account of Chand Kaur's death and of Nau Nihal Singh is confused, so left out.

The entry says Kindattu took the last king of Ur captive; the article says Ishbi-Erra captured Ibbi-Sin. Who captured him is left out. Leick makes Idaddu I a son of Pepi rather than of Kindattu; not printed.
The article gives his death as 24 August 1858 in the lead but as the 16th after a collapse on 8 July in the body (lunar and Western calendars mixed); only July 1858 and the year are printed.
The entry calls Sighnaq the capital of the White Horde; the article says the Blue Horde. Neither name is printed.
The entry's height of about 12 metres is not in the article; not repeated.
The article gives his death as 24 April 1664 in the lead and 26 April 1664 in the text; the day is left out. The article is short; nothing added beyond it.
Left out: the possible 1046 expedition (Annals of Lindisfarne and Durham), Gospatric's Writ and Cumberland, the Durham estates, the Domesday figures and the Máel Coluim debate, for length.
Characterisations of Ne Win's rule (totalitarianism, xenophobia) left in the scholars' mouths or out; the regime ended in 1988, so this is history, not a verdict on a present government.

The article gives no date for the temple; the entry's 14th century BCE is not contradicted. Article says Lepsius 'discovered and described' the site in 1844 but also that Major Felix visited in 1829; only 'described' used.
The article is partly built on older texts (Smith-style passages); its claims on the lower and higher assemblies are muddled, so only the Council of the Four Hundred and the appeal are used.

The article dates the Vadakalai-Tenkalai schism to around the 16th century in its lead and around the 18th century in its texts section; no date given. Nathamuni is placed in the 10th century in the lead and 'likely in the 9th century CE, or the 10th' later; no century given. Ramanuja's century left out (entry: 11th and 12th centuries; article: 11th century). The lead says the Telugu Sri Vaishnavas are not divided into Vadakalai and Tenkalai, while a later section lists them as a Tenkalai branch; left out.
The article calls Kearny's government in New Mexico a 'military dictatorship' that overthrew a democratic state government; contested framing, left out.

The article says the Assyrians conquered Israel and Aram-Damascus; the entry says Tiglath-pileser took Damascus and annexed much of Israel's territory. The conquest of Israel is left out so as not to contradict the entry.
Plutarch's two figures for the size of a mess (about 15 men; Agis's 15 phidites of 400 or 200) are given only in their first form.
The article says the tablet was in seven fragments with the bottom right corner missing; the entry's eight pieces, one missing, agrees.

The article's section on 1815 is muddled (it speaks of the Acts of Mediation and a renamed Federal Assembly in the restoration period); only its clear points are used. The dates of the Sonderbund War are left out (article: 1845 to 1848).

The article dates the Vishnu temple to the 8th century CE; the entry dates the Tamil inscription to the ninth century. No date given. The article's 'city states dating back to Srivijaya times in the 13th century' is confused and left out.
The article's lead speaks of his 1828 visit; the text says he visited in 1828 and lived there the following year, which agrees with the entry's 1829.

SKIPPED: the article has under 250 words of substance beyond the list of its seventeen founders and adds little to the description The article says that from 1964 the party was called the Tanzania African National Union; unsourced and not used.

The article says reports of the island were known before Alexander the Great, as inferred from Pliny; the entry says Greek writers learned of it after Alexander's campaigns. Left out. The entry says Ptolemy's map greatly exaggerated the island's size; the article does not say this and it is not repeated or contradicted.

The article says the suspension of 1881 lasted 'the next seven years' but ended in 1883; the length is left out. Adoption date: the article gives 28 April [O.S. 16 April] 1879, the entry 16 April; no date given here.

The article gives the birth of his daughter Eleanora as 15 July 1883 in one place and 1885 in another; no year given. He was relieved as Chief of Staff on 19 May 1918 (the lead says until 18 May 1918); the end date is left out.

The article gives 20 February 1524 as his death in the lead but says the Kaqchikel annals place it at the battle of 12 February 1524; no day given for his death. The article gives a birth year of 1499 without a source in the text; left out.
The article calls Iltani's husband Aqba-aḫum of Qaṭṭara and Aqba-hammu of Karana in the rulers' list; written Aqba-hammu throughout.
Scholars dispute whether Long Ya Men was Keppel Harbour, the main Singapore Strait or the Strait of Lingga; I kept the article's 'thought to be' hedge and left the debate out.

The article dates the fire to 394 BCE (Pausanias), the entry to 395 BCE: date left out. The article says the site was a focal point from the 10th century BCE, the entry 'by the 8th century BCE': left out. The article calls Scopas a 'Parian architect'; the entry calls him a sculptor: role not restated.
The entry says Ruz reached the tomb in 1952; the article says he removed the slab in 1952 and that the stairway, cleared two years later, led into the tomb. Years left out of the discovery paragraph.
Left out the article's last line on the Christchurch mosque shootings and the 1966 Max Mathews and biochemistry-song items for length.
The article gives his death as 743 without 'c.'; the entry has d. c. 743: no year given in the text. Battle of Guadalete year (711 or 712) left out as unnecessary.
SKIPPED: the article has under 300 words and adds little beyond the entry (birthplace, ranks, a railway and a memoir)

The entry names the castle's builder Hugh of Saint-Omer and dates it around 1105; the article calls him Hugh of Fauquembergues and gives both 1105 and 1106. Builder's name and year left out. Left out the article's unsourced claim of Canaanite origins and the speculation on crusader descent.

The entry says the scholars were led by al-Zarqali under al-Mamun; the article says only that the tables were partly based on his work and that the team is largely unknown apart from him. Leadership and patronage not restated.
The count's title is spelt Castenheira as in the article (usually Castanheira).
The entry states he later went on pilgrimage to Jerusalem; the article says only that, according to Snorri, he may have left for the Holy Lands or may have died. Left out of the text.
The article names the playwright only as 'B. v. Beskow'.
The article says the clock face was originally painted by Paolo Scazzola in 1483, before the mechanism of 1583-1588 (probably a slip for 1583): left out.
Left out the present-day statistics, accident list, rehabilitation projects and high-speed rail plans.
The minstrel's name is spelt Walter von der Vogelweide as in the article (usually Walther).
SKIPPED: the article has about 250 words and adds only the sums paid and a few lines of significance to the entry

The article gives the indemnity inconsistently (4 million reis converted from 2 million caroli guilders in the lead, eight million guilders in the History section); the entry says four million cruzados, paid partly in salt. No figure printed for the final indemnity. The article says Portugal 'ceded' Ceylon and the Maluku Islands; kept as the article gives it, but the editor may wish to check (the VOC had conquered them).
The article calls the pamphlet 'Letters in Miranda' and dates it 1796, before the treaty; written as 'Letters to Miranda' without the year. The editor may prefer the article's form.
The article says the Union of Grodno of 1566 joined the Duchy of Livonia to Lithuania and that after 1569 it was a Polish-Lithuanian condominium; left out for length.
The entry dates the fortress to around 980 and names Harald Bluetooth; the article agrees (timber felled 980, built presumably 981).
Left out the article's paragraph on the Second Vatican Council, which does not concern the Articles.

SKIPPED: The article has under 250 words of substance, mostly on the modern municipality; its archaeology section adds little to the description and nothing on the Greek city or the treaty with Knossos.

The article dates Alvarado's defeat of the Tzʼutujil near Panajachel to 1523; the entry says 1524. Neither year printed. The entry says the kingdom dates from the 13th century; the article says only the post-classic period (c. 900-1500). Not printed. Left out the 1980s guerrilla violence paragraph: the article frames it oddly ('as part of the Guatemalan genocide, guerilla violence'), and the 2005 Hurricane Stan deaths.
The Panna Dai story is told as fact in the article and is written so here.
The article gives the father's name as both Thorgil Sprakling and Thorgils Sprakalägg/Thorkel Sprakalegg; the first form is used.

The article gives the region's bounds as the Swabian Jura, Lake Constance and the Lech, and says the eastern border is now usually the Iller; the entry says the Danube, the Iller and Lake Constance. Bounds not repeated.

The article gives his birth as c. 1733 (lead) and 1730 (Early life); neither printed. The length of his reign is given as about three months (lead) and ten days (body); the entry says within weeks. Only the dates 12 May and 1 June 1758 are printed. The tomb is placed northeast and northwest of U Bein Bridge in two places; direction not printed.

The article also places western parts of Vanga in West Bengal (the Presidency division and possibly Burdwan and Medinipur) and its core between the Padma-Meghna and Bhagirathi-Hooghly; the entry calls it south-eastern Bengal, roughly central and southern Bangladesh. Only the Bangladeshi part is printed. The Vijaya story is told as fact in the article; attributed to 'the story of Prince Vijaya'.
The entry calls it former forest of the princely state of Bansda; the article does not mention the princely state. Not repeated.
'a diagram of how the surviving copies descend' is an explanation of 'stemma' not given in the article; the editor may cut it.
The article dates the end of his presidency to 28 June (resignation), 29 June (term) and 30 June 1871 (ousted); no day of his fall printed.

The article says the Sringeri matha dates ordination to 1331 and Rosen Dalal to 1377; left out. The entry says the Sringeri monastery was founded by Adi Shankara; the article treats the founding of the four mathas by Shankara as a story that may date from the 16th century, and Hacker as doubting the mathas existed before the 14th century. Not printed either way.

The article both says the Front was founded in February 1977 by merger and lists a Vietnam Fatherland Front founded in 1955; the entry gives 1955 and the 1977 absorption, which agrees with the second reading. No assessment of present political life is given.
The article spells the state Bushahr; the entry Bashahr. The article says he was elected nine times to the assembly in the lead but seven in the body; left the count out.
The article's early medieval paragraph on Powys and Llys Pengwern is garbled; left out apart from the dated facts.
The article dates his self-declaration as Grand Master to 1525 but his election as Deutschmeister to 1526; the year of the declaration was left out.
The article does not give the Treaty of Xanten's division of the lands (the entry's Cleves, Mark and Ravensberg for Brandenburg), so no terms are printed.

The article's lead gives c. 1092 to 9 August 1135, its body birth around the turn of the twelfth century and death sometime between 1134 and 1148; the entry dates him only fl. 1120s-1130s, so no birth or death date is printed. The entry's monastery at Stolpe is not in the article; only the memorial stone is mentioned.
